surface_summary: Two brothers, Salter and Noah Quick, are found murdered hundreds of miles apart, each carrying money and valuables untouched but having been searched. A mysterious tobacco-box with cryptic scratches and a blood-stained handkerchief are key clues. The investigation uncovers a stolen monastic treasure hidden on the Northumbrian coast and a gang including Netherfield Baxter, a Frenchman, and Chinese accomplices seeking to recover it.
accepted_facts: Salter and Noah Quick were murdered on the same night at distant locations
Both men carried money and valuables that were not stolen
A tobacco-box with cryptic scratches was found on Salter Quick
Netherfield Baxter and accomplices bought a yacht and sought the treasure
inferred_conclusions: The murders were committed by the same individual
The tobacco-box scratches directly reveal the treasure's exact location
The murderer was not among the known conspirators
mechanism_description: The murders were committed by members of a criminal gang seeking stolen monastic treasure hidden near the graves of the de Knaythevilles on the Northumbrian coast. The Quicks were killed because they possessed rubies and pearls from the treasure. The gang included Netherfield Baxter, a Frenchman, and Chinese accomplices. Internal betrayal among the Chinese crew led to a deadly fight aboard their yacht, resulting in multiple deaths and the escape of Wing, who helped the captives.
delivery_path: Netherfield Baxter and accomplices steal monastic treasure and hide it near de Knaytheville graves
Noah and Salter Quick come into possession of rubies and pearls from the treasure
The gang tracks and murders the Quicks to obtain the jewels
Mr. Cazalette discovers clues including the tobacco-box scratches and blood-stained handkerchief
The gang steals the tobacco-box and pocket-book to conceal evidence
Wing infiltrates the gang to protect captives and gather intelligence
A mutiny among the Chinese crew leads to a deadly fight and the destruction of the yacht
outcome_result: The gang is destroyed in a fight aboard their yacht, the treasure is recovered, and the surviving conspirator Wing is found wounded but alive.

false_assumption.statement: The murders were committed by a single unknown man who followed Salter Quick to the Northumbrian coast.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The simultaneous murders and the presence of two sets of footprints at Salter Quick's murder scene suggest a single assailant. The initial suspicion falls on a mysterious man seen asking about Netherfield graves.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It obscures the fact that multiple conspirators from a gang were involved, and that the murders were coordinated but carried out by different individuals with different motives.

false_solution.accused_suspect: The man who met Salter Quick at the inn (James Beeman's stranger)
supporting_points: He was seen asking about Netherfield graves near the time of the murder
He was a stranger to the area and seemed suspicious
The footprints suggested a light-footed person, possibly a woman or this man
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was not seen again and had no motive or opportunity to commit the murders

red_herrings.description: Locals believed the light footprints at Salter Quick's murder scene were made by a woman, suggesting a female murderer.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The light footprints were actually made by one of the male conspirators wearing light-soled boots.

red_herrings.description: Mr. Cazalette's secretive behavior with the blood-stained handkerchief and tobacco-box led to suspicion he might be involved.
red_herrings.points_at_suspect: Mr. Cazalette's odd actions and possession of clues
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was investigating the case out of curiosity and lost his pocket-book to thieves; he was not involved in the murders.

closed_circle.rationale: The suspects are limited to the known conspirators who bought the yacht, had access to the treasure, and were present at the crime scenes; no other plausible suspects appear.

time_anchors: March 8, 1912 - Leonard Middlebrook arrives at Ravensdene Court
time_windows: Night of March 9-10 for Salter Quick's murder
Night of March 9-10 for Noah Quick's murder
Three weeks before arrival at Hull for yacht purchase
trust_channels: Dr. Lorrimore and his servant Wing

inference_path.observation: Salter Quick was murdered but his money and valuables were untouched.
inference_path.correction: The motive was not robbery but possession of a secret or treasure.
inference_path.effect: Focus shifts to secret or hidden valuables as motive.
required_evidence: Police report on Salter Quick's body showing money and valuables present
Inspection of Salter Quick's clothing showing pockets turned out

inference_path.correction: The scratches represent a map or plan related to the treasure.
inference_path.effect: Leads to investigation of monastic treasure and its location.
required_evidence: Photograph of tobacco-box lid with scratches
Mr. Cazalette's notes and enlargements of the photograph

inference_path.observation: No Netherfield graves exist near Ravensdene Court.
inference_path.correction: The name Netherfield was confused with de Knaythville, the actual ancestral name.
inference_path.effect: Search focuses on ruins and graves of de Knaythville family.
required_evidence: Local parish records and history books
Inscription on tombstone of Humphrey de Knaythville

inference_path.observation: Two men, Baxter and Frenchman, bought a yacht and sailed north.
inference_path.correction: They intended to recover the hidden treasure near Ravensdene Court.
inference_path.effect: Yacht and crew become suspects and focus of police search.
required_evidence: Ship broker Jallanby's testimony about yacht purchase
Yacht Blanchflower found at Northumbrian coast

inference_path.observation: A fight and multiple deaths occurred aboard the yacht.
inference_path.correction: Internal betrayal among conspirators led to deadly mutiny.
inference_path.effect: Identifies multiple culprits and explains deaths aboard yacht.
required_evidence: Eyewitness accounts of fight and deaths on yacht
Bodies found aboard yacht including Baxter and Chinese crew

inference_path.observation: Wing, Dr. Lorrimore's servant, was missing from the yacht.
inference_path.correction: Wing escaped wounded and sought help, acting against conspirators.
inference_path.effect: Wing is revealed as a double agent aiding captives.
required_evidence: Wing found wounded at Dr. Lorrimore's house

inference_path.observation: Rubies and pearls were found with Wing after escape.
inference_path.correction: These jewels were the motive for the murders of the Quicks.
inference_path.effect: Confirms treasure as central to the murders and conspiracy.
required_evidence: Jewels recovered from Wing after rescue

discriminating_test.design: Wing is allowed to escape from the yacht and is tracked to Dr. Lorrimore's house where he is found wounded but alive. The presence of the silk cap and recovered jewels confirm his identity and role. The test reveals whether Wing is a conspirator or a double agent.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: Wing was the fourth Chinaman on the yacht, escaped after a mutiny, and acted to protect the captives and expose the conspirators.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: Wing is found alive with the silk cap and jewels, confirming his identity and innocence.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all essential clues: the tobacco-box with scratches, the blood-stained handkerchief, the inventories of the monastic treasure, the testimonies of witnesses like Solomon Fish and James Beeman, and the detective's investigations. The presence of the yacht, the crew, and the mutiny are all described. The reader can deduce the motive, the conspirators, and the sequence of events leading to the murders and the final confrontation.
